pages.subtitle: P1-02 / Sort, match and order / Mr Aliyu leads.

elements.text: Objective. Sort collections and compare small sets. Also retain the source ordering practice within 1 to 5. Read all pupil text aloud. Prerequisite: count objects to five; revisit the Chapter 1 model as needed. The pupil pages have no numbered instructions.

Concrete start. At a reachable table, provide three clean, large leaves and five large, clean tops. Use pieces too large to swallow; supervise use. These are pretend tickets and counters, not food. Sort by type in front of pupils, then invite them to sort a separate tray. A set means a collection. Reuse this same three-leaf/five-top tray for the ending. No pieces are added or removed.

Model, practise, compare. Enact p. 2 with real pieces before using the pictures. On p. 3 pair two tops with four, one to one, and point to the two unmatched tops. Name more and fewer. On the equal-row activity, invite a prediction, then match: all three have partners in both rows, so the sets have the same number even when spaced differently. On p. 4 count the dot sets 2, 3, 4 before connecting them to numerals. Read the numerals aloud.

Observe and help. Confuses type with colour: restate leaves together/tops together, sort one, then ask the child to place another. Counts twice: move each counted object aside. Chooses by row length: bring one object beside one partner. Gives a partner twice: physically move paired objects together. Cannot order: build sets of 1, 3 and 4, then compare adjacent sets. Recheck each difficulty with fresh small sets; accept speaking, pointing or moving objects before writing.

Recall and fresh checks. On p. 6 wait before offering help. After support, change the quantities (for example 1 and 2) and ask again. For this recheck, 2 has more and 1 has fewer. Keep p. 7 fresh tasks independent before feedback. On another day, ask what Mr Aliyu showed. Give four leaves and two tops to sort and compare, then ask pupils to order 5, 2, 3. Answers: leaves/tops; four leaves more, two tops fewer; 2, 3, 5. Record independent / with help / not yet.

Every example and added task
p. 1 tray and p. 2 sort model: 3 leaves and 5 tops. Guided sort: the leaf in the second position is already circled; point to the leaf in the fourth position. Tops are first and third. Grace moves her leaf to the leaves.
p. 3 model: 2 matched pairs, 2 unpaired tops in the four-set; 4 more, 2 fewer. Guided rows: 3 in each, every top has a partner; same number. Any one-to-one bijection is valid.
p. 4 model: 2, 3, 4 dots in increasing order.
p. 6 support: 2 pairs and 1 unmatched lower dot; lower set of 3 has more. Accept either valid line from the remaining upper dot to a free lower dot.
p. 7 resolution: 3 pairs, 2 spare tops; tops more, leaves fewer. Put those 2 unmatched tops in a real spare box. Read the closing dialogue after doing this action.

P1-02-Q5 (p. 6): Exactly five objects.
P1-02-Q6 (p. 6): Match one to one or count both sets.

elements.text: Sequence. Pupil textbook pages 1-6: classroom purpose; two-to-none demonstration and the meaning of 0; guided one-to-none, recognition, numeral formation and empty-box drawing; independent source tasks; recall/support; actual packing resolution and fresh checks. Use the existing book introductions; this continuation does not repeat them.

Prepare. Large safe counters, reachable tray/mat, storage box, pencil/paper and ordinary cards 0-5. Demonstrate each physical action. The trays/boxes in exact diagrams are containers, not counted tops. Never count decorative classroom artwork. No subtraction or equality notation is needed in these pupil pages.

Notice. Separate empty-set meaning, recognition, independently naming a numeral, and writing without copying. A child may count the tray as one: ask what is being counted, then inspect its contents. An open or reversed loop needs formation practice, not a judgement that the child cannot understand none. Accept usual communication for naming; use an established adapted writing method where needed.

Intervene, then recheck. Use one counter and another container. Model moving it away and checking the contents. Link none to 0. Recheck independently with two counters and a fresh tray, both put away: zero remain. For writing, air-write and trace a large closed loop, cover the model, then dictate zero on blank paper. Give specific feedback and retry later.

Delayed recall. Next session put three counters in a different basket, then ask the pupil to put all away: zero remain. Mix cards 2,0,4: independently name two, zero, four without an adult supplying the names. Cover them and dictate zero: write 0. Record meaning, recognition, naming and formation separately; give further supported practice if needed.

elements.text: Sequence. TB1 purpose; TB2-3 quantities six/seven then eight/nine, numeral names and one-to-one counting; TB4 live formation/air-writing; TB5 actual sorting; TB6 modelled quantity order and source tasks; TB7 drawing model, recall/support; TB8 actual sorting/counting/ordering resolution, then fresh checks. Do not advance before each quantity is secure. Existing introductions remain in the opening book.

Prepare. Reachable mats, large safe counters, paper/pencil and cards 1-9. For S002 prepare 6 blue circles, 7 red squares, 8 green triangles and 9 yellow non-square rectangles. Model sorting by outline; shape naming is not assessed. Printed pieces use one colour to show the outline rule. All 30 pieces stay in the same four story groups. Squares remain a special kind of rectangle; use the most specific names here.

Separate skills. Observe quantity, count-once method, recognition, independent naming, dictation/formation and order separately. Counting correctly does not prove reading; copying does not prove writing from dictation. For reversed 6 or 9, keep paper upright and watch the loop/downstroke. Accept usual communication and established adapted writing methods.

Support/recheck. Use counted/uncounted mats and five counters plus one. Model six, then independently check a new seven set. If sorting is hard, sort two small groups then rebuild the target groups. For numeral difficulty, air-write/trace one form, cover it, then dictate it; later retry a different order. Do not label a child as the weak counter.

Delayed recall, next session. Count fresh sets of 6, 7 and 8. Read shuffled cards 9, 6, 8, 7 independently. Dictate nine, seven, six, eight: 9, 7, 6, 8. Order 8, 6, 9: 6, 8, 9. Sort 7 tops and 9 leaves; state each count. Record which skills need support.

elements.text: Source tasks. P1-04-Q1 (TB6/WB2): 7. Q2 (same): 8. Q3 (same): 6, 7, 8, 9. Q4 (TB7/WB3): exactly 6 separate dots, any clear arrangement. Q5 (same): exactly 9 real objects, each counted once; state 9. Q6 (TB7/WB4): recount 8 once per object; the last word is eight. Moving each counted object is valid. Check the method as well as the total.

Every model. TB2: 6 is five and one; 7 is five and two. TB3: 8 is five and three; 9 is five and four. Spreading changes no quantity. TB4/WB1: recognisable 6, 7, 8, 9; loop below for 6, above for 9. TB5: 6 round/7 square; guided 8 triangle/9 rectangle. TB6: pairing 6 and 7 leaves one unmatched in 7; seven goes between six and eight. Before/after mean earlier/later in counting order. TB7: 2 counters/2 dots; support 6, recheck 7. TB8: groups of 6, 7, 8, 9 in increasing row order.

S002 (TB5/WB5). Mix all 30 pieces. Sort by outline, count and record: 6 circles, 7 squares, 8 triangles, 9 non-square rectangles. Order: 6, 7, 8, 9. Observe actual sorting; written counts alone do not demonstrate it. For story closure (TB8), verify all 30 pieces in these groups before starting the pretend game.

Fresh checks (TB8/WB6). Privately prepare new scattered groups of 8 and 9; answers 8 and 9. S003: count 9 objects once each, then independently name ALL shuffled cards 1-9 without supplied names. Test recognition separately by naming 6, 7, 8, 9 in a different order. Before dictation, cover ALL cards, printed numerals and the pupil's handwritten count answers, including the totals on WB6. S004: dictate eight, six, nine, seven; answers 8, 6, 9, 7, correctly oriented. Do not show answers or read this rubric aloud while testing.
Same tasks on both surfaces count as one check. New physical objects, independently shuffled naming and covered-model dictation are fresh evidence. No tasks have been administered to pupils.

lessons.title: Equal halves and quarters
lessons.goal: Recognise halves and quarters of objects and shapes.
lessons.look: Zainab folds a paper sheet to share its space. Must fair pieces be equal?
lessons.learn: A half is one of 2 equal parts of a whole. A quarter is one of 4 equal parts. Equal means the same amount. Unequal pieces are not halves or quarters.
lessons.worked: Fold a rectangle in half. Fold again into 4 equal parts. One part is a quarter.
lessons.play: Fold scrap paper into halves, then quarters. Shade a half on one sheet and a quarter on another. Point to half and quarter of a paper model of a fruit.
lessons.hint: Use paper instead of food. Accept different equal-area partitions.

questions.prompt: How many equal parts make halves?
How many equal parts make quarters?
Draw two equal halves of a rectangle.
questions.answer: Rectangle divided into two equal-area parts.

questions.prompt: Draw a square and shade one quarter.
Explain why your shaded part is a quarter.
questions.answer: The whole has four equal parts and one is shaded.

lessons.title: Put small sets together
lessons.goal: Add two or three small sets.
lessons.look: Musa has 2 tops. Amina gives him 1 more. What happens to his set?
lessons.learn: Addition puts amounts together. The sign + means add. The sign = means has the same value as. Count all objects to find the total.
lessons.worked: 2 + 1 = 3. Two tops and one top make three tops. 1 + 1 + 2 = 4.
lessons.play: Join two sets with 1 to 3 tops each, keeping totals below 5. Then join three small sets. Say and check each number sentence.
lessons.hint: Read the whole sentence aloud. Equals states the same value on both sides.

questions.prompt: 1 book and 3 more make how many?

questions.answer: Both combine one and two objects to make three.

lessons.title: Count on to add
lessons.goal: Add two or three numbers with totals to 18.
lessons.look: The friends join sets. Can they start counting from the larger set?
lessons.learn: Keep one number in your head and count on the other amount. Adding zero leaves the number unchanged. Check by counting all the objects.
lessons.worked: 8 + 5: start at 8; count 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. So 8 + 5 = 13. For 3 + 2 + 4, first make 5, then add 4 to get 9.
lessons.play: Make sums with tops. First keep totals below 10, then try up to 18. A partner checks by grouping ten and ones.
lessons.hint: Keep every total within 18. Use objects before mental calculation.

questions.prompt: 7 seeds and 5 more make how many?

questions.answer: Count fourteen objects, or count on six from eight.

lessons.title: Add tens and ones
lessons.goal: Add two-digit numbers without regrouping, to 40.
lessons.look: Class bundles hold ten sticks. Can we add bundles and loose sticks separately?
lessons.learn: Line up tens with tens and ones with ones. Add the ones. Add the tens. Here each ones total stays below ten, so no new bundle is needed.
lessons.worked: 23 + 14: 3 + 4 = 7 ones; 2 + 1 = 3 tens. Total 37. Check with bundles.
lessons.play: Build 12 and 15 with bundles and loose strips. Join tens and ones. Make another sum with a total no greater than 40.
lessons.hint: Align places. Do not read 23 as two plus three.

questions.prompt: 22 pencils and 11 more make how many?

questions.answer: Two tens plus one ten and three ones make three tens and three ones.

lessons.title: Take away
lessons.look: Musa puts some tops back in a box. Is the number on his mat getting larger or smaller?
lessons.learn: Subtraction can take away. The sign − means subtract. Count what remains. Or count backwards one step per removed object.
lessons.play: Place up to 18 tops on a mat. A partner removes some while you watch. Say the subtraction and check by putting them back.
lessons.hint: Keep removed objects visible so pupils can undo the action.

questions.prompt: 12 chalk pieces: use 3. How many remain?

lessons.title: Find a missing part
lessons.goal: Find unknown numbers and check everyday calculations.
lessons.look: Amina sees 3 tops. Some are hidden. There are 7 altogether. How can she find the hidden part?
lessons.learn: A blank stands for a missing number. Find the value that makes both sides equal. Use objects or count on. Check by reading the completed sentence.
lessons.worked: 3 + __ = 7: count 4 more. The blank is 4. __ − 2 = 5: start with 7, since 7 − 2 = 5.
lessons.play: Hide part of a set of up to 9 tops. Tell the whole and the visible part. Then make an everyday story about books with a missing amount.
lessons.hint: Vary blank positions. Check by substituting in the original sentence.

questions.answer: Use 5 in the blank and verify 4 + 5 = 9.

lessons.title: Pretend coins and change
lessons.goal: Identify coin values and calculate with pretend kobo.
lessons.look: Daniel makes paper tokens for a pretend shop. Why does a value label matter?
lessons.learn: Nigerian money is called naira and kobo. 100 kobo = 1 naira. Use labelled pretend tokens: 1k, 5k, 10k and 25k. These are historical-value exercises, not real prices or a claim about money circulating today.
lessons.worked: 5k + 10k = 15k. Pay 10k for a pretend 6k item: change is 10k − 6k = 4k.
lessons.play: Draw token outlines and label values. An adult may show a genuine coin for identification and supervised pencil tracing. Never mark or alter real money.
lessons.hint: Use large paper tokens. Real prices and currently used denominations differ.

questions.prompt: Why read a token value, not just count tokens?
questions.answer: Different tokens can have different values.

lessons.title: Longer, shorter and farther
lessons.goal: Compare and order lengths and measure with body units.
lessons.look: Zainab compares two strings for a garden bed. Where should their ends start?
lessons.learn: Line up one end to compare. Longer means more length; shorter means less. Measure with equal hand spans or footsteps placed end to end with no gaps or overlaps.
lessons.worked: One string is 4 of Amina’s spans; another is 6 of her spans. The second is longer by 2 of her spans.
lessons.play: Measure a table in your spans and a safe path in your steps. Record whose units you used. A seated child can use a paper strip instead.
lessons.hint: Body units vary. Do not compare different pupils’ counts as if their spans were equal.

questions.prompt: Lengths are 3 and 5 equal strips. Which is longer?
Draw a line longer than your finger.
questions.answer: Line exceeds that pupil’s finger length.

questions.prompt: A path is 8 steps out and 8 back. Total?
Measure a book with repeated paper-strip units.
questions.answer: Practical count, same unit repeated without gaps.

questions.prompt: Why line up the string ends?
questions.answer: So the other ends show the difference fairly.

lessons.title: Our day in order
lessons.goal: Sequence everyday activities and use time words.
lessons.look: The friends describe a school day. What could you do before coming to school?
lessons.learn: Time helps order events. Morning comes before afternoon. Evening comes before night. Routines differ. Use before and after to describe a day.
lessons.worked: In Amina’s story: wake up, wash, eat, then go to school. Eating is before going to school.
lessons.play: Draw three routine cards. A partner puts them in your chosen order. Tell a story using first, next and last.
lessons.hint: Accept varied home routines. No pupil must disclose private home details.

questions.prompt: Which comes first: morning or afternoon?
In Amina’s story, what follows washing?
Explain before with your own two events.
questions.answer: The first event occurs earlier than the second.

lessons.title: Heavy and light
lessons.look: Musa lifts an empty bag and a bag with books. Which feels heavier?
lessons.learn: Heavier and lighter compare weight. Size alone does not tell weight. Use small safe objects on a simple balance. The lower pan holds the heavier load.
lessons.worked: On a balance, a stone side goes down and a leaf side goes up. The stone is heavier than the leaf.
lessons.play: With an adult, balance a small stone, eraser and leaf. Predict, compare and order. Lift only light safe items.
lessons.hint: Never ask pupils to lift heavy loads. Use observed results, not appearance.

questions.prompt: Which is heavier in the example?
Which is lighter in the example?

questions.answer: Suitable example such as a leaf.

questions.prompt: A balance is level. What can this show?
Compare two safe objects and record a result.
Does bigger always mean heavier? Explain.
questions.answer: No; a large empty box can be lighter than a small stone.

lessons.title: Solid shapes around us
lessons.goal: Name and sort cubes, cuboids, cylinders and spheres.
lessons.look: Daniel explores a ball, a box and a closed tin. Which can roll?
lessons.learn: A sphere is ball-shaped. A cube has six equal square faces. A cuboid has six rectangular faces, with opposite faces matching. A cylinder has two flat circular faces and a curved surface.
lessons.worked: A dice models a cube; a cereal box models a cuboid; a closed straight-sided tin models a cylinder; a ball models a sphere.
lessons.play: Sort clean safe objects by solid shape. Test rolling and stacking. Remove sharp tins and small choking hazards.
lessons.hint: A cube is a special cuboid. Use a clear non-cube cuboid for initial comparison.

questions.prompt: What solid does a ball model?
Which solid has six equal square faces?
What solid does a closed straight-sided tin model?
Sort a ball and box by smooth rolling.
questions.answer: Ball rolls smoothly; box does not.
Cube edges are all equal; the chosen non-cube cuboid has unequal adjacent edge lengths.

lessons.title: Flat shapes and patterns
lessons.goal: Match and name circles, squares and rectangles.
lessons.look: Amina traces a box face. How does the flat drawing differ from the box?
lessons.learn: A circle has a curved boundary and no corners. A square has 4 equal straight sides and 4 square corners. A rectangle has 4 square corners and opposite sides equal. A square is a special rectangle.
lessons.worked: Circle, square, circle, square is a repeating pattern. A turned square is still a square.
lessons.play: Trace safe flat faces. Match shapes after turning them. Make a repeating pattern for a pretend cloth border. Find square and rectangular faces in the classroom.
lessons.hint: Orientation does not change a shape. Compare with a non-square rectangle.

questions.prompt: How many corners has a circle?
How many equal sides has a square?

questions.answer: Four right angles, opposite equal sides, unequal adjacent lengths.

questions.prompt: Name an object with a rectangular face.
questions.answer: Suitable example such as a book.

questions.prompt: What stays the same when a square turns?
questions.answer: Its four equal sides and four right-angle corners.

lessons.title: Find out about our class
lessons.goal: Collect and record ages and heights.
lessons.look: The friends discuss how children grow. What could they record respectfully?
lessons.learn: Data are pieces of information. Ask the same question each time. Record age in completed years. Compare heights from floor to head with marked paper strips. Use letters instead of names.
lessons.worked: Invented practice data: pupil A is 6 years, B is 7, C is 6. Two pupils are 6 years old.
lessons.play: Use the invented records or collect voluntary ages privately. Compare paper height strips without ranking children as better or worse. Record height with a consistent method.
lessons.hint: Participation is optional. Do not publish identifiable child data. Fictional data are acceptable.

questions.prompt: How old is practice pupil B?
Order the practice ages from least.
Name a tool for comparing heights.
questions.answer: Marked paper strip or suitable measuring tape

questions.prompt: Why ask everyone the same age question?
questions.answer: To compare answers about the same thing.
